newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-From the Beehive-Hurdles to govt for Left.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-From the Beehive-Hurdles to govt for Left.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Oct 8 - Just when New Zealand voters look set to elect a left-of-centre coalition government, one of the key elements, the Alliance, has raised the bar over which its two coalition partners Labour and New Zealand First will have to leap if the governor-general is going to sign all three into office.
The Alliance, if it holds the balance of power, will demand higher taxes on the wealthy, and tariffs on imports. It also wants to axe market rentals on state houses.
Labour may go along with raising taxes on the wealthy, but disagrees that tax increases should start with people earning $28,500 a year or more.
And increasing tariffs is anathema to Mike Moore, who built his reputation as Overseas Trade Minister as a leader of the Cairns Group driving for lower tariffs and free trade.
NZ First has come out against abolishing market rentals on state houses, and reducing the accommodation supplement, because that penalises people in the private sector rental housing.
Alliance leader Jim Anderton believes Labour should make it clear which policies a post-election coalition would adopt.

He says the reason Labour leader Helen Clark is ruling out pre-election talks is because she knows several MPs would walk away from the party, no matter which way she went. "The Labour caucus is deeply split, and its leadership prefers those who are going to leave to wait until after the election."

Former Labour prime minister David Lange lends credence to the Anderton theory, accusing Helen Clark of being "totally dishonest" to give people the impression she could form a government: she might have time to form a minority government, but that was the extent of it, he said.
Ms Clark was, he said, surrounded by disloyal "blue-eyed twits".
Despite these Lange-isms, the Clark camp is buoyant, and foresees another wriggling victory from television's worm.

The opposition leader, on course to become New Zealand's first woman prime minister, can date the turning point in her campaign to the "worm", which scored a clear win for her in the first leaders' debate.
National's strategists are in despair at the prospect of the worm again turning against Prime Minister Jim Bolger.
They shrivel at the evil fortune that has put them in thrall to such a mindless creature.

And it does not ease the pain that three parties, who have spent the past three years slagging each other as much as the government, are soon to join each other in picking up the reins (and perks) of office.

One theory already alive in the Beehive is that far from engaging in coalition talks that could spread over the next four or five weeks, the Clark-Peters duo will take charge within 24 to 48 hours, apportioning out key areas of responsibility to their own MPs for management during the transition process and indicating the prospect of reshuffle once the formal coalition deal has been agreed.
Peters is said to have his eye on being deputy prime minister, and he would probably insist that his deputy Tau Henare should take the Maori Affairs portfolio, as well as possibly Labour.
Peter McCardle would also be expected to get a portfolio, probably Employment and Immigration.
On the basis that Labour would have twice as many MPs as NZ First, Peters could hardly demand more than seven cabinet positions in a 20-person cabinet.
He himself has called for the number of cabinet posts to be reduced to 15.

A Labour-NZ Frist coalition would still need support on critical votes in Parliament from the Alliance, and would have to come to some arrangement with it, even though the Alliance has said it would not enter into a "formal" coalition.
According to Anderton, the Alliance would be "forced to defend" Labour's policies if it entered a formal coalition or accepted Cabinet posts.
Such sensitivity would not limit Peters -- but though he might join Labour initially, the question is whether the arrangement would be long-lasting.
The scenario might be that once National down the track a year or two had moved to replace its current leadership, Peters and NZ First would be free to reappraise the options.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters.)
